source.title: Understanding Scaling Laws with Statistical and Approximation Theory for Transformer Neural Networks on Intrinsically Low-dimensional Data

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures held-out test loss across data-size and model-size sweeps and fits log-log scaling exponents, using new datasets and model suites.
record.gate_note: The empirical scaling plots and their textual descriptions are included. The paper's theoretical bound is for squared regression error; it explicitly leaves a cross-entropy loss error bound for future work. The Figure 3 GPT-2 empirical exponent is taken from Kaplan et al., so that cited result is not recorded as this study's own result. Figure 4 measures estimated intrinsic dimension, not loss, so its architecture ablations are not rows for these claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study pretrains 125M GPT-style models across three orders of dataset size on three corpora and fits log-log lines to test loss. It also fits model-size scaling of Pile test loss for the Pythia suite. These are its own power-law loss measurements, compared against an intrinsic-dimension-based prediction.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that intrinsic data dimension governs transformer scaling exponents. Their theory predicts empirical data-scaling exponents within ±0.02, generally slightly overestimating them. It underestimates model-scaling exponents, possibly due to under-training or data entropy. Estimated intrinsic dimension is relatively stable across embedding-model size, width, depth and context length.
record.recipe_differences: Uses log-log fits of test loss against data or model size, but applies them to new datasets and model suites and compares observed exponents with intrinsic-dimension-based predictions.

fits_no_version.finding: The estimated intrinsic dimension of token embeddings changes only mildly with embedding-model size (15.56 to 20.02), embedding width (15.56 to 18.68) and context length (15.86 to 12.9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The intrinsic dimension of the data, estimated from embeddings, predicts the scaling exponents, with predicted alpha_D within ±0.02 of observed.

record.problems: The plotted curves do not provide exact per-dataset or Pythia exponents in the text. The empirical predictions use the simplifying assumption of Lipschitz regularity (β = 1). The paper explicitly leaves a theoretical bound for cross-entropy loss to future work; it describes test loss as comparable to squared error.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were omitted. The GPT-2 empirical exponent in Figure 3 is referred to Kaplan et al. (2020), rather than reported as a result from this study. Figure 4's intrinsic-dimension ablations do not measure loss or directly test a listed claim version.

untested.parts: Compute scaling (explicitly left to future work); model-size scaling beyond the Pythia suite; non-bottleneck conditions for data sweeps run at a single 125M model size.
Not tested: no small-run fit is used to predict much larger runs.
Not tested: the architecture ablations measure estimated intrinsic dimension, not loss.
Not tested: text pretraining only (code SQL is still text-like pretraining).
Dependence on parameter counting, schedule or fitting method, and curvature away from a power law, are not tested. Only dependence on the dataset is shown.

missing.what: Exact per-dataset empirical exponents alpha-hat_D, predicted alpha_D and estimated intrinsic dimension for each dataset
Exact empirical Pythia exponent alpha-hat_N and the model-size range used

record.verdict_notes: The paper is primarily theoretical (squared-error regression bounds). Its empirical support for V1 is modest: one model size for the data sweeps, and figure-only values. Table 1's GPT-2 and Chinchilla exponents and the GPT-2 alpha-hat_N are cited from Kaplan, Sharma and Kaplan, and Hoffmann, so they are not this study's results. Peer review status: the record lists NeurIPS, while the arXiv v1 says 'under review'.

versions.untested_parts: The empirical sweeps test data-size and model-size scaling, not compute scaling; they do not establish that the other quantities are non-bottlenecks in every regime.
No small-run fit is reported as a prediction of loss on runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute-budget allocation sweep or loss-minimising parameter/token split is tested.
Architecture ablations measure estimated intrinsic dimension, not loss at fixed parameter count.
No other modality, repeated-data regime, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling experiment is reported.
The paper does not test whether fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits vary with fitting choices or setup, or whether loss curves bend away from a power law.

rows.subject: 125 million parameter GPT-style LLMs on OpenWebText
rows.operation_detail: Pretrained a series across dataset sizes and fit a log-log line to test loss versus data size.
rows.measure: Empirical data scaling of test loss; fitted exponent α̂D.
rows.note: The text says the three datasets have nearly log-linear laws, with exponents between 0.1 and 0.15 overall. It does not assign an exact exponent to this dataset. Its predicted exponent overestimates the empirical exponent but is within ±0.02 absolute error.
rows.check: The text calls all three datasets' laws nearly log-linear, with exponents between 0.1 and 0.15. OpenWebText has the smallest exponent. Exact values are only in Figure 2. Model size is fixed at 125M, so this is data scaling only; the text does not show the model is not the bottleneck. Also bears on V7, since the exponent differs by dataset.
